passage: Vijay came back on a Monday in September after three months off, and I watched him do it carefully. He had told the team he would work half-days for the first week, and he kept to it: gone by one, no arguing. He asked for the heavy budget review to be moved to the following week. He had a ten-minute check-in with our manager on Thursday and wrote something in a small notebook afterwards. Once I saw him stop mid-sentence in a meeting, breathe, and say, "I need five minutes." He stepped out and came back steadier. I can't say what he felt in those moments. He looked a bit tense, a bit determined. But he treated his tiredness like a gauge on a dashboard, not something to shout down. - Anirban

Friday, before the return. Asif sits with a notebook after six weeks off. "If I go back full speed on Monday, I'll be back where I started by the fifteenth," he says aloud to his wife, Rukhsar. He writes: Week 1, half-days, 10 to 2. No budget meetings until week 2. Wednesday, check-in with Chetan.
Wednesday, week one. At 1.30 his head feels thick and he notices he has read the same paragraph three times. The old Asif would have pushed on. He writes "energy dip, 1.30" and logs off at 2 as planned. At the check-in he tells Chetan, his manager, what he has noticed.
Monday, week three. Full days now. When he feels that thick-headed tiredness creeping in before the long review, he takes a ten-minute walk first instead of ignoring it.

qa.q: What hours did Asif plan for the first week?
What is Asif worried about when he says he'll be back where he started?
qa.a: He is worried that rushing back at full speed will exhaust him again, so he feels cautious about the return.

qa.q: What else could Asif try if the dips keep appearing in week three?
qa.a: He could ask Chetan to keep long reviews away from his low hours for a while, or stretch the gradual restart.

qa.q: How does the plan look to Chetan as the manager?
qa.a: Chetan gets honest updates at the check-in and a clearer picture of Asif's energy, which makes planning his workload easier.

grounding: It shows a man planning a return with half-days, no heavy meetings at first and a manager check-in, and reading his energy dips as signals.

subtype: Approach: emotion-aware pacing of the return [Thinking]
passage:
Farhan sir put down his chai when Nilesh said he was going back to work on Monday, full days. "Beta, let me tell you about my own return, long ago. I had been off three months, exhausted. I was twenty-six and wanted to prove I was fine. But the night before, I sat and thought: if I walk straight into the Monday board meeting, I will drown.
So I asked my manager for half-days the first week. I kept away from the big meetings for ten days. And every evening I wrote one line: how tired, from one to five. When it reached four, I stopped for the day, no argument with myself. On Friday I showed my manager the notebook.
By the third week I was back fully, and I stayed back. That notebook told me when to slow down before I crashed."

qa.q: What did Farhan write each evening?
qa.a: One line: how tired, from one to five.

qa.q: What was young Farhan feeling the night before returning?
qa.a: He was anxious and afraid of drowning in the Monday board meeting, even while wanting to prove he was fine.

qa.q: Which choice in Farhan's story mattered most, and why?
qa.a: Stopping for the day whenever the tiredness score reached four, because it treated his energy as a signal before he crashed.

qa.q: How might Farhan's manager have seen the notebook on Friday?
qa.a: The manager could see real information about his energy, making it easier to trust the half-day plan and judge when to add more.

grounding: It shows a young man pacing his return with half-days, no big meetings early and a manager check-in, using his tiredness as a signal.
